results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the Drosophila [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database. VFB records show that the mushroom body is divided into these three main parts: the calyx, which receives sensory interneuron afferents; the pedunculus, a thick axon bundle; and the mushroom body lobe system, which consists of a vertical branch and a medial branch. VFB holds various data related to the mushroom body, including images, neurons with different types of connections to the mushroom body, parts and subclasses of the mushroom body, and lineage clones found in the mushroom body.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila brain contains several types of Kenyon cells. VFB records show that there are subclasses of [Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"), including [[KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain")(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), KCab-c, [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Kenyon cell of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). According to the VFB neuron taxonomy summary, the main subtypes of Kenyon cells are alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which are further subdivided into subtypes such as core, surface, posterior, anterior-posterior, middle, and dorsal. VFB holds [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") records of subclasses of Kenyon cell, indicating the diversity of Kenyon cell types in the adult Drosophila brain. To explore the different types of Kenyon cells in more detail, you can query the available VFB data, such as the list of images of Kenyon cell, scRNAseq data for Kenyon cell, or transgene expression in Kenyon cell.

results.title: Basic connectivity
results.question: What are the main input neurons to the mushroom body?
results.response: The main input neurons to the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are sensory interneurons, according to VFB. VFB records show that the calyx, which is closest to the cortex, receives sensory interneuron afferents. Additionally, VFB indicates that the main input neurons to the mushroom body include projection neurons from the antennal lobe, as well as sensory interneuron afferents to the calyx and neurons with presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body, including larval antennal lobe multiglomerular projection neurons and larval uniglomerular projection neurons. VFB holds [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") records of neurons with some part in the mushroom body, [601](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in mushroom body") records of neurons with synaptic terminals in the mushroom body, and [366](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPresynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with presynaptic terminals in mushroom body") records of neurons with presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body, which may provide further information on the inputs to the mushroom body.

results.question: What brain regions does the antennal lobe connect to?
results.response: The [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") connects to the mushroom body and lateral horn. results.title: Cell count
results.question: Approximately how many neurons are in the adult Drosophila central brain?

Additionally, VFB records show more than 125,000 neurons, but the source of this count is not specified as a published total with a citation. Therefore, the 9413 neuron types annotated in VFB are the most specific data available from VFB. For further information, you can explore the available VFB data, which includes Parts of adult central brain and Transgene expression in adult central brain.

**Published neuron-count estimates — adult central brain** (from the literature):

- more than 125,000 neurons (adult Drosophila central brain connectome/model) — A Drosophila computational brain model reveals sensorimotor processing. — PMID 39358519
- ~139,255 neurons (whole adult Drosophila brain) — Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain. — PMID 39358518

_VFB has annotated 9,413 neuron types with some part in adult central brain — a curated annotation count, not the biological total._

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response:
The Drosophila central complex is a structure in the insect brain that has been studied for its role in various functions. According to general training knowledge, the main components of the Drosophila central complex include the ellipsoid body, the protocerebral bridge, the noduli, and the fan-shaped body. 

VFB does not currently hold specific data on the functions associated with each of these components. However, it is known from the literature that the central complex is involved in functions such as spatial memory, visual navigation, and locomotor control (as discussed in publications like 10.1038/nrn2348 and 10.1016/j.neuron.2013.01.010). 

For more specific information on the functions of the central complex components, further queries can be directed towards available datasets and publications. VFB holds various datasets related to the Drosophila brain, but the specific functions of the central complex components would need to be looked up in the literature or other databases.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response: The LPLC2 visual neuron type is a type of visual neuron with specific characteristics and functions. According to VFB, its cell body lies in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind. The neuron has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer, allowing it to detect looming stimuli. In the lobula, it has its main dendritic arbors in layers 4 and 5B, with minor processes in layer 5A, and presynaptic sites in layer 4. Its arbors span approximately 25 lobula optic columns, overlapping with other LPLC2 cells. The LPLC2 neuron projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4. VFB records show that the activity of LPLC2 neurons elicits a jump escape response. VFB holds that there are approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe and that they are cholinergic. VFB does not currently hold comprehensive data on all connections of the LPLC2 neuron type beyond its projection to the PVLP and its dendritic arborization in the lobula and lobula plate. Follow-up queries can be used to explore the available data on the LPLC2 neuron type's connections and function in more detail.

results.question: Trace the anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure. What is each level in the hierarchy?

This information comes from the VFB database, which provides the anatomical containment hierarchy. 
VFB holds multiple records for the containment hierarchy, but all of them include the adult antennal lobe, adult deutocerebrum, adult cerebrum, adult central brain, and adult brain as part of the hierarchy.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior and has a distinct anatomy and connectivity. It can be identified by its large descending axon, which is several times larger than any other axon in the cervical connective, and enters the cervical connective via the posterior cerebro-cervical fascicle, descending on the ipsilateral side. The giant fiber neuron has dendritic arborization in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center, where it receives substantial input from zone A and B Johnston organ neurons. It also arborizes in the posterior ventrolateral protocerebrum and gorget. 

VFB records show that the giant fiber neuron has specific genetic tools, including available driver lines such as P{R48A11-GAL4.DBD} and P{R68A06-GAL4.DBD}. The connectome data indicates that the giant fiber neuron has downstream connectivity classes for DNp01, with [389](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records annotated in VFB, and upstream connectivity classes for DNp01, with [472](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records annotated. 

Relevant publications that mention the giant fiber neuron include Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), and Namiki et al. (2018). VFB holds [23](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") images of DNp01, [5](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,SplitsTargeting "Run in VFB: Splits targeting DNp01") splits targeting DNp01, and [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01. 

For further information, you can explore the available images of DNp01, examine the splits targeting DNp01, or investigate the transgene expression in DNp01, all of which are available in VFB. You can also query the downstream and upstream connectivity classes for DNp01 to gain a deeper understanding of its connectivity.
